The heater ticks at your knee, its grille a dull orange, the first warmth of the night reaching your shins. The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam and throws the whole shed white, end to end. Thirty feet away, at the far end, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, his hands at his sides, his face to the plank.

You slide the dead datapad into the backpack on your back. Your left hand comes away empty. You touch the comm at your collar and the hiss there stops. The channel is closed. Nothing more goes out.

You lift a hand toward the heater.

"Heater's on. We're warm, we're lit, we're barred. We use the time."

Wick looks round at you. Then back at the door. He says nothing.

On the cot the two folding knives lie side by side on the creased blanket, heavy. You pick one up in your right hand. It is closed, and it has weight to it, a work tool, not a toy. The other stays where it is, beside the hand lamp and the coveralls.

"Come back here, Wick. Take a knife. You keep it on you from now on."

He does not turn. "In a minute."

He stays where he is.

"While you're at it, try some of these clothes on. You're going to need protection."

"Later." He says it to the door.

The second knife stays on the blanket. The coveralls stay where they lie, four sets, with the boots and the gloves.

Then, faint through the boards, from far down the rise:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words, the same way. It comes in through every gap the light goes out through.

Wick does not move. His shoulders draw up and settle. Under his breath, so low it barely crosses the thirty feet between you:

"Hear through it."

The heater ticks. The light hums. Outside, the night goes on.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. The heater ticks at your knee. Thirty feet up the shed, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, his face to the plank.

"Stay on the door if you need to. I'll bring the knife to you."

"Yeah." He says it to the door. He doesn't turn.

You put the folded knife away in a pocket of your robes. Both hands come away empty.

The coveralls lie in a heap on the creased blanket. You spread them out one by one. Heavy work cloth, a name stencilled across each back: HADDOW. PELL. VARRO. G. TOLLIVER. All four are cut for grown men. All four are stiff at the knees and the cuffs with dried clay, pale grey, that cracks and sifts onto the blanket when you bend the cloth. VARRO's breast pocket gives up a stub of yellow marking chalk. HADDOW's, a balled pair of glove liners. In PELL's hip pocket your fingers find a fold of flimsi: a stores chit. 1 x cell, hand lamp. Signed Pell. Never stamped as filled.

PELL's set is the smallest. It is still long in the leg and wide in the shoulder for a boy of sixteen. The boots are all men's boots. You take PELL's coveralls and gloves in your left hand and leave the boots where they stand.

You walk the twenty-five feet up the shed. Wick hears you come and doesn't turn. You set the coveralls and the gloves on the workbench, an arm's length from him, and say nothing.

He looks down at them. Then at you. Then back at the door. He doesn't touch them.

You walk back down the shed to the cot.

The hand lamp is a squat crew work lamp, a barrel with a lens screwed onto its end. You pick it up in your right hand and thumb the switch. It clicks. Nothing. You click it again. Nothing.

With your left hand you unclip the glowrod from your belt, still lit, cool white across the blanket. You unscrew the lamp's lens. The flat cell tips out of its well into your palm, and you set it down on the cot. The glowrod goes into the barrel in its place. It is a close fit; you turn it, ease it down, and it seats. The lens screws back down over it. Light throws out of the lamp's mouth in a beam across the back wall.

You unscrew the lens again, switch the glowrod off inside, and screw the lens back down. The lamp goes dark in your hand. You put it in a pocket of your robes. Your own light is out now. The glowpanels still hold the whole shed in white.

Fifteen feet up the shed, at the hauler's nose, the charging lead hangs coiled on its post. You lift it off and push the plug into the sled's socket. It seats.

The gauge stays dark. No light comes up on the driver's stand. Nothing shows that it is charging. The key sits in its switch, turned to off.

Faint through the boards, from far down the rise:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

Wick stands where he is, facing the door. Under his breath:

"Hear through it."

You walk the ten feet to the workbench. The coveralls lie where you left them, beside him. Above the bench the site chart hangs on its pin, flat and white under the strip light: the shaft drawn straight down under Silo Three's base, the cramped column of depths beside it, the deepest written 13.5. You go over it again, line by line. Nothing more comes out of it.

While you are still bent over it, the voice comes again. The same words. The same breath before them.

Wick does not move. "Hear through it."

You straighten up. He is five feet from you, close enough to see the muscle working in his jaw.

"Your mum, before she went. Did she take anything with her? A light, a tool?"

He doesn't answer at once. When he does, it's to the door.

"Her coat. Nothing else." A breath. "She didn't even take a light."

The heater ticks at the far end of the shed. The strip light hums. Outside, the night goes on.

details.text:
The strip light hums under the roof beam. Five feet from you, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, his face to the plank. PELL's coveralls lie on the workbench where you left them.

You walk the twenty-five feet down the shed to the cot. The heater ticks there, its grille a dull orange. On the creased blanket, between the flat cell and the folded coveralls, lies the second knife. You pick it up in your right hand. Heavy, folded, the handle worn smooth.

You walk back up the shed and hold it out to him.

Wick takes it. He thumbs it open once and looks at the blade under the light, then folds it and pushes it into the front pocket of his trousers.

"Thanks."

"Those are yours now. Get them on over your clothes. Roll the cuffs."

He looks down at the coveralls on the bench. PELL, stencilled across the back, upside down from where he stands. He doesn't touch them.

"Later."

"The hauler won't show a charge. Did the crew ever have trouble with it?"

"Never saw it stop." To the door. "It ran every day till they stopped."

You walk the ten feet to the hauler's nose. The sled waits on its stand, its bed still crusted with dried earth and broken grey stone. The lead runs from the post into its socket. The gauge on the driver's stand is a dark glass eye.

You work at it for three minutes. The plug is seated. The wall socket is live. You draw the plug, look into the socket, seat it again. You run your fingers along the lead, tap the gauge, look for any light anywhere on the stand. There is none. Whether the fault is in the lead, the gauge or the sled's cell, you cannot tell.

While you are bent over the stand, the voice comes, faint through the boards, from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

Behind you, a scuff on the packed earth. Wick has stepped to the door. Both his hands are on the plank. He stands there with his weight against it, not lifting, not moving. Then he takes his hands away and steps back.

You turn the key from off to on.

Nothing. No light on the stand. No whine from the repulsors. The sled does not stir on its stand. The key sits at on in a dead machine.

"Pell put in for a lamp cell and never got it. Who hands out stores at the Grange?"

"The Warden." He doesn't look round. "Everything goes through her. Cells, seed, fuel. She counts it all." A pause. "She said cells were for the winter."

"No light, out into that. She meant to come straight back, Wick."

He says nothing. He stays facing the door, fifteen feet from you, the knife a hard square in his pocket.

"You said that the Grange had a long range communicator? We may need to try there again before we go to Silo 3 - I need to get in touch with backup."

"In her office." Flat. "She won't let you near it."

He says nothing more.

The voice comes again. The same words, the same breath before them, far off in the dark beyond the boards.

Wick does not move. Under his breath: "Hear through it."

The heater ticks at the back of the shed. The strip light hums. Through every gap in the boards, the shed's light lies out across the gravel for anything to see.

details.text:
The heater ticks at your back, its grille a dull orange. At the far end of the light, thirty feet up the shed, Wick sits on the edge of the workbench in PELL's coveralls, an arm's reach from the barred door.

On the cot: the flat cell, the coveralls, the boots, the gloves. You take the cell, a dead slab no bigger than your palm, and push it into a pocket of your robes beside the lamp. Then the gloves, three pairs, stiff with old dirt at the fingertips, folded and pushed into the other pockets until the robes hang heavier on you. The coveralls and the boots you leave where they lie.

"Does the Warden keep sled cells at the Grange, or just lamp cells?"

Wick answers down the length of the shed. "Cells. I don't know what kind. She keeps them in the store room and counts them out."

You walk up the shed, past the dead hauler on its stand, to the bench.

As you reach him, the voice comes through the boards from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

His gloved hands close on his knees. Under his breath: "Hear through it."

You draw the blaster from the holster on your right hip with your left hand. It comes up into the white light, heavy and familiar.

"Those fit you better than I thought. Keep the gloves on."

"Okay."

You turn the pistol round and take it by the barrel, the grip offered to him, the muzzle toward your own wrist and the floor.

"You have the knife as a backup but if you're gonna go out there with me: I want you to feel confident that you can protect yourself. This blaster is mine, but if we survive the night I'll get you one that can be yours to keep."

He looks at it. He looks at it for a long moment, the grip a hand's width from his knee, and his hands stay where they are.

"I've never shot one."

The blaster stays in your hand.

You reach for him through the Force. It comes clear and close, as it has each time tonight. Fear, and under the fear a tiredness that goes all the way down. The pull from the rise is still there, an ache that tightens at each call, and he leans against it like a man leaning on a door. Shame, fresh and hot, as the grip hangs in front of him. And beneath all of it the thing he has kept to himself since the gate: settled, quiet, held against something, still leaning toward the trees. Under that, the guilt you felt before, close to the surface.

With your right hand you take the lamp out of your pocket. It sits dark in your palm, the glowrod seated behind its lens. The blaster is still in your left hand, held by the barrel, the grip toward him.

The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. The plank sits across its brackets an arm's length past Wick's shoulder. Outside, beyond the boards, the rise is quiet again.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left. The lamp sits dark in your right hand. In your left, the blaster, held by the barrel, the grip a hand's width from his knee.

"That's all right. Nobody's born knowing how."

You keep it there.

"If you can shoot a rifle, a blaster isn't much different. You aim at the thing you want to shoot and you pull the trigger. You only fire if you are sure you want to shoot the thing. I believe in you. I need you to believe in you. Your fear only holds you back."

He looks at the grip. He does not move.

You say the Code to him, low and even. "There is no emotion; there is peace." Line after line, to the end. The heater ticks at the back of the shed. Wick listens with his eyes on the blaster and says nothing until you finish.

Then you show him. You turn the pistol in your left hand and point with the fingers of the hand that holds the lamp. The grip. The trigger, and the guard around it. The line along the top you sight down. The muzzle kept to the floor. The finger laid flat along the frame, outside the guard, until he means to fire. Three minutes, slow. Nothing is fired.

When you finish, he reaches out and takes it by the grip.

It sits wrong in his gloved hand at first, too big for him. He lifts it anyway, sights along the top at the back wall, at the stack of panels by the empty lockers, his finger lying flat outside the guard. He holds it there a breath. Then he lowers it, the muzzle to the floor, away from you both.

"Okay."

Your left hand is empty now. The lamp, still dark, is in your right.

The voice comes through the boards from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

He goes still. His eyes go to the door, to the plank, to the white light leaking through the gaps in the boards. He does not speak. The blaster stays low in his lap, the muzzle on the floor.

The rise goes quiet again.

"You've been holding something back since the gate. What is it?"

For a long moment he doesn't answer. Then, to the door, not to you:

"When the door opened I was going to go. To the trees. To her." He swallows. "I wasn't going to tell you."

You reach for him through the Force. It comes clear and close, as it has each time tonight. Fear, and the tiredness under it, all the way down. The pull from the rise is still there; he leans against it as he has all night. But something in him has steadied since his hand closed on the grip. And now, with the words out of him, a raw relief, as if he has set down something heavy. The settled thing he has carried since the gate has moved. It no longer leans toward the trees. It leans toward the door: he is waiting for it to open. Under it, the guilt you felt before has eased. Lighter, now that it is said.

"When we go to the Grange, you walk where I tell you. Every step."

He looks up at you. The blaster is low in both his gloved hands, the muzzle to the floor.

"Every step."

The strip light hums. The heater ticks. The plank sits across its brackets an arm's length past his shoulder, and beyond the boards, the rise is quiet.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left. The lamp sits dark in your right hand. Wick sits on the edge of the bench in PELL's coveralls, the cuffs rolled, your blaster low in both gloved hands, the muzzle on the floorboards.

"Thank you for telling me. That took more than holding the blaster."

For once he does not look at the door. He looks at you.

"Yeah." Barely more than breath.

"If she's out there, where would she go? Where did she work, where did she walk?"

He thinks about it. The heater ticks at the back of the shed.

"The drying floor. She'd go there before anywhere." He tips his head toward the back wall, past it. "The long barn. Other side of the silos from here. Hundred feet, maybe."

He says nothing about where she walked.

"Did you see anything when she walked outside? What direction she went?"

His thumbs move on the grip and go still.

"Out the door. I saw her back, and then she was out of the light. I didn't see which way." A breath. "Nothing. Just her. It was dark."

Then, from far down the rise, thin through the boards:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Wick is on his feet before the last word, turned to the door, the blaster hanging low at his side, muzzle down. His shadow lies across the plank. He does not touch it. You can hear him breathing, short and fast through his nose.

The voice does not come again.

After a moment he sits back down on the edge of the bench, the pistol low between his knees, muzzle to the floor, and stares at the plank.

The light goes out through every gap in the boards, into the dark.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left. The lamp sits dark in your right hand. Wick sits on the edge of the bench in PELL's coveralls, the cuffs rolled, your blaster low between his knees, the muzzle on the floorboards.

"The drying floor. Is there a way to that barn from here that keeps us off the open lane?"

He answers at once, as if he has walked it in his head already.

"Out the door, straight across the lane to the silos. Thirty feet." His chin points at the door. "Then between them, round the back of Three. There's a gap you can get a cart through. You come out at the long barn's end." A breath. "The lane outside the door's the only open bit."

Then, quieter: "There's a small door at that end. It slides. They never latch it."

His breath is short, fast through his nose. You can hear it over the heater.

"Breathe with me. Slow. It'll call again, and it'll be the same words."

He looks at you sideways. You breathe in, slow, and out, slower. On the second breath he follows, ragged. On the third it is closer to yours. By the sixth his shoulders have come down off his ears. His gloved fingers loosen on the grip; the muzzle stays on the boards.

"Same words," he says, under it.

You wait. The heater ticks. He says nothing more.

"You stood up and you didn't touch the plank. I saw that."

He looks at the floor between his boots.

"I wanted to."

"Which night did she go out? Before the dogs went wrong, or after?"

"After." He stops. His thumb moves on the grip and goes still. "I don't know which night. After."

Nothing else comes.

Then, from far down the rise, thin through the boards:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The catch on "honey". The fall at the end. Every syllable where it was.

Wick does not get up. His jaw tightens. He breathes in through his nose, slow, the way you showed him, and out.

"Same words," he whispers.

The voice does not come again. The strip light hums. White light leaks out through every gap in the boards, into a dark you cannot see.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left and the switch box on the frame beside it. The lamp sits dark in your right hand. Wick sits on the edge of the bench in PELL's coveralls, your blaster low between his knees, the muzzle on the floorboards.

"Wanting to is fine. You didn't. That's the part that counts."

He looks at you. Then he nods, once.

"Okay."

"Keep breathing like that. In slow, out slower. It works on Jedi too."

He does it again with you. In, slow. Out, slower. His shoulders stay down. He says nothing.

You put the lamp into the pocket of your robes. Both hands free. Then you take it out again, unscrew the lens, find the glowrod's own switch with your thumb and press it. Cool white light jumps across the floorboards and up Wick's boots. You screw the lens back on and push the lamp, lit, back into the pocket, lens to the cloth. A dull white glow shows through the weave at your hip and lights nothing.

"Before we go back to the Grange, we look for your mom in the long shed. You said behind Silo number 3, correct?"

"The long barn." He says it fast. "Round the back of Three, yeah. At the end."

Then he looks up at you, properly, for the first time since he sat down.

"Before the Grange? You mean it?"

"If we go, we go together. Door, lane, silos, the gap. You stay at my shoulder and you don't run, whatever you hear."

"At your shoulder." His gloved thumb moves on the blaster's grip and stops. The muzzle stays on the boards. "What if it's her?" Quieter. "What if it's really her out there?"

He does not get up.

"That gap behind the silos. Is it lit at all? Anything back there to trip on, or hide in?"

"No lights back there." He shakes his head. "Ruts from the carts. Nothing to hide in but the dark."

You reach across to the switch box on the door frame and work its latch with your fingers. The cover swings open on its hinge. The lever stays up.

Inside: the lever's contacts behind a clear guard plate. Below them, three breakers in a row, each with a worn stamped tag, all three up. Thick cable comes in at the bottom from the wall and leaves at the top for the roof beam. No scorch. No smell of burning. Nothing you can see is wrong.

Then, from far down the rise, thin through the boards:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The catch on "honey". The fall at the end. Every syllable where it was.

Wick's jaw tightens. He does not move from the bench.

"Same words," he says, under his breath.

The strip light hums. White light leaks out through every gap in the boards, into a dark you cannot see.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left and the switch box open on the frame beside it. The lamp glows dull white through the cloth at your hip. Wick sits on the edge of the bench in PELL's coveralls, your blaster low in both gloved hands, the muzzle on the floorboards.

"If it's her, we bring her back. If it isn't, we come back here. Either way, you're with me."

He nods. He says nothing.

You slip a strap off your shoulder and swing the pack round, find the canteen by feel and shoulder the pack again. The cap turns under your thumb. The water is cold and tastes of the bottle. You hold it out to him.

He looks at it a moment. Then he moves the blaster into his right hand, muzzle still to the floor, and takes the canteen in his left. One swallow. His throat works. He does not give it back; it rests on his knee in the glove.

"It's all right to hope. Just keep breathing while you do it."

"Trying."

"If she isn't on the drying floor, where's the next place she'd go?"

"The byre, maybe." He looks at the canteen, not at you. "She'd check the animals." A pause. "I don't know."

The pack comes round again. Two sealed field rations, foil-cold. You shoulder the pack, tear one open with your teeth and start on it: dense, salt, faintly sweet. The other you hold out to him.

"Gotta eat, we're going to need the energy when we get moving. Regardless of what we find in the next building, we need to be on alert and focused. From there we go back to the Grange and call the Order and see if we can get a signal out to the detail that should have been with me."

You chew. Swallow.

"You're doing great kid, just breathe."

He sets the canteen down on the bench beside his hip, takes the ration with his free hand and rips the foil open with his teeth. Then he eats fast, head down, the way people eat when they had forgotten they were hungry. Between bites, not looking up:

"If they come. Your Order." The foil crackles in his fist. "If anyone comes."

Then, from far down the rise, thin through the boards:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

He goes still, the ration halfway to his mouth, and looks at the door. He says nothing. After a while he finishes eating. He wipes his gloves on the coveralls and takes the blaster in both hands again, muzzle to the floor.

"When we go: I lift the plank, you hold the blaster low and stay at my left. Nobody answers the voice. Not one word."

"Low. Your left." He swallows. "Not a word."

You point at the lever in the open box on the door frame. You do not touch it.

"I'm leaving the lights on. If we had anything reflective I would be lighting up the whole damn town. I'm not worried about them seeing us, I don't like the fact that we can't see them and they're smart enough to follow pace with our footsteps."

Wick's eyes go to the walls. White light leaks out through every gap in the boards into the dark. He looks at it for a long moment and says nothing.

You watch him. His jaw, his hands on the grip, the way his breath goes. He is scared, plainly; under the fear there is something else, and it is hope. He wants it to be her. And he is holding himself to what he told you, by force, the way you hold a door shut against wind.

"The long barn. Will anyone be on the drying floor this late, or should it be empty?"

"Should be empty." He says it to the floor. "Nobody works it after dark."

You hold out your hand. He picks the canteen up off the bench and puts it into it. You close your right hand round it.

The voice comes again, faint, from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Every syllable where it was.

His jaw tightens. He keeps his eyes off the door. No words.

You lean in to the switch box and look it over closely in the full white light: the guard plate over the lever's contacts, the three breakers in their row, all up, the worn stamped tags, the thick cable in at the bottom and out at the top. You look for most of a minute. Nothing you can see is wrong.

You swing the cover shut with your left hand and press the latch home. The lever stays up. The strip keeps humming.

One step and you are at the door. The plank sits across both brackets in front of you, rough grey wood at the height of your chest. Behind it, the boards, and behind them the lane, the silos, the dark. You do not touch it.

"You ready?"

The bench creaks. Wick stands, the blaster low in both hands, the muzzle to the floor, and comes to your left side, an arm's length off, where you told him to be.

"Ready."

His breath is slow and careful. In. Out, slower. The canteen is cold in your right hand. Somewhere down the rise, the voice is quiet, for now.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the shed door, the plank across both brackets an arm's length in front of you, the switch box shut and latched on the frame at your side. Wick stands at your left, an arm's length away, in PELL's coveralls, your blaster low in both gloved hands, the muzzle to the floorboards. The lamp glows dull white through the cloth at your hip. Behind you the heater ticks.

You slip a strap and swing the pack round. The canteen goes in, stoppered, among the rations. The pack settles on your back again. Both your hands are empty.

"Thanks for eating. That was the hard part, and you did it."

A short nod. Nothing else.

You look at him. Really look: the cuffs rolled four times, the gloves too big, the grip held exactly the way you showed him.

"I don't know your parents. You've only spoken about your mom. But I would bet all my credits that they would be damn proud to see you, right now. You take feedback well, you listen to instruction, and you're clearly intelligent and competent. You'd make a good soldier or engineer. You're too young now, but I hope you consider joining the republic in some capacity when you come of age. Maybe we can work together again someday."

He looks down at the blaster. Colour comes up in his face, plain under the white light, from the collar of the coveralls to his ears. He says nothing. His thumbs move once on the grip and go still.

You watch him a few seconds longer: the set of his mouth, his hands. He is embarrassed. Under it he is scared. Past that, nothing you can read.

"Whatever it says out there, it's only words it's heard. Hold on to that."

He nods.

You put a hand on his shoulder. Under the coverall cloth he goes stiff, shoulders up, the way a body braces before it is struck. Then, slowly, he lets the hand stay. You hold it there a moment, looking at him; then you let go.

Outside, nothing. No voice. Only the light leaking out through every gap in the boards into the dark, and the dark taking it.

You turn to the plank.

"On three. I lift, you stay left. One, two..."

Wick sets his feet at your left. The blaster stays low in both hands, the muzzle to the floor. His eyes are on the plank. He draws a breath and holds it.

The plank sits across its brackets, untouched. The door is still barred.

details.text:
"Three."

The word stays in the shed with you. You get both hands under the plank and lift: it comes up out of the brackets heavier at one end than the other, the old shoring wood rough through the cloth of your sleeves, and you stand it on end against the wall beside the empty brackets. Nothing holds the door now but its own weight. Wick is at your left, an arm's length away, the blaster low in both gloved hands.

You kick it.

The door goes out on its iron hinges and slams back against the outer boards of the shed, a crack of wood on wood that goes out across the lane and keeps going. In the same breath your right hand takes the saber off your left hip and the blade comes alight with a snap and a low, steady hum, indigo, an arm's length of it, throwing its colour over the doorframe and the gravel at your feet.

You step out.

Five feet onto the lane. The cold comes in through the robes at once. Behind you the strip light floods out of the open door in a long white fan across the gravel, across the cart ruts, almost to the base of the silos thirty feet ahead: three dark shapes standing up out of the light into nothing, Silo Three the middle one. Past the edge of the light there is no grass, no fence, no field. There is only black, and the blade's hum, and your own breath.

Wick comes out with you. Low, at your left, an arm's length away, the blaster held down, his eyes on the dark. He does not say a word.

"If we get separated go to the Grange - the Warden will let you in and for the love of the force: Breathe."

Your voice goes out into the open with nothing to stop it.

"The Grange," Wick says. Then he breathes out, slow, the breath he has been holding since the count, and it smokes in the light.

Then it comes. From far down the rise, clearer out here than it ever was through the boards, every breath in the same place:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Wick goes rigid at your left. His mouth comes open. He does not answer. He does not move.

The words die away down the slope. The heater ticks somewhere behind you in the empty shed. Out past the light, nothing moves that you can see.

details.text:
Your left hand goes into the robe pocket and comes out with the lamp. The lens has been against the cloth all this while; out in the air its beam jumps from your palm, cool and white, a hard straight shaft beside the blade's indigo hum.

"Grab your lantern before we go - blaster in your dominant hand, lantern in your off hand."

Wick does not answer. He turns and goes back through the doorway, past you, into the light. Ten feet: the foot of the workbench, where you set his lantern down more than an hour ago. It is still there, still open, its flame standing straight behind the glass. He crouches, takes it up by the bail in his left hand, the blaster in his right, and comes back out the way he went. He stops at your left, an arm's length away. The shed is empty behind you, the heater ticking to nobody.

You wait until he is there. Then you look.

The beam goes where your eyes go. In the shed's white spill the lane lies bare: gravel, the old cart ruts, then the curved bases of the three silos thirty feet ahead, standing up out of the light into nothing. The beam goes over them and between them and finds grass. Long grass, knee-high and more, pale in the light and black at its roots, deep enough to hide something lying flat in it. Nothing in it moves while the beam is on it. When the beam moves on, you cannot tell.

To the left, the welding cart still leans against the left-hand silo where it was left, torch and bottles on its bed. Under Silo Three's welded seam, the grey spatter of slag on the gravel.

No sound out there. Only the blade's hum at your right hand, and the heater behind you.

"Wick. Look at me. Those are only words it's heard."

He looks at you. Lantern light from below, the gloves too big on his hands, the coveralls rolled at the cuffs. He says nothing.

You go still and reach out, past the light, into the dark, for anything living besides the two of you.

Nothing comes back. Nothing you have ever been taught finds a living thing out there; what you can feel through the Force is a disturbance, a great one, and there is none. The dark stays exactly as dark as it was.

"With me," you say, low. "Low, my left. We go now."

You cross. Wick comes at your left, low, an arm's length off, the lantern swinging in his left hand, the blaster in his right. Twenty-five feet of gravel. The shed light thins under your boots and stops at the foot of the silos, and you stop with it, at the edge, where the white runs out.

Up close the silos are wide and tall, their curved walls rising out of the light into black. Between Silo Three and the right-hand silo is the gap: cart-wide, gravel and packed earth chewed by old ruts. You put the beam into it. It runs along Silo Three's back wall as the wall bends away out of sight, and at the far end it finds no wall, no building. Only more dark.

Long grass on both sides of you at the silo bases. Nothing moving.

Then the beam comes back down to your boots, and to the dust at the gap's mouth.

Prints. Fresh, pressed deep, each one wider than your hand. More than one animal. They go into the gap and through, toward the back of the silos, toward where the beam cannot follow.

You look at the lamp in your hand and weigh it. Thrown with any aim it would carry twenty feet. Sixty, at the most, and then it is gone. Nothing you have can bring it back to you.

"Alright, Wick, this is it," you say, low. "You tell me where we're going and I'll get us there. Periodically keep a check behind us. Where you look is where your lantern goes. That's actual fire in there, right?"

"The gap," Wick says. "Round the back of Three, then along to the end."

He looks back over his shoulder, down the lane the way you came, and the lantern goes with his eyes: the yellow swings across the gravel, the open door, the empty white shed. Then it comes forward again.

"It's fire. Lamp oil."

He looks back once more before he faces the gap. The light swings out behind you and back. Ahead of you the gap stands open and black, the prints going into it, and past the edge of the light nothing moves that you can see.

details.text:
You go down on one knee at the gap's mouth and put the beam on the dust.

The prints hold still under the light. Each one wider than your spread hand, four toes and a heel pad, and at the front of every toe a hard little hole where a claw went in. They are pressed over the old cart ruts, not under them. Two animals. No more than two: one set laid down, the second stepping almost into the first, one behind the other, at a walk. Nobody hurried through here. And every print points the same way, into the gap. Nothing comes back out.

The edges are crisp. No wind has softened them, no dust has settled in the claw holes. Tonight. Within the last half hour or so.

You stand.

"What did you say happened to the dogs?"

"They went wrong." Wick's voice is flat and quick. "Tore the hangar door out from inside. Never came back in."

"Did you say that there was a way to the Dryer by going through Silo 3?"

"Not through it. It's welded." He lifts the lantern toward the gap, and the yellow light leans into it after the white. "Round the back of it."

"Slow. Lantern up. One step at a time."

He brings the lantern up to his shoulder. He does not say anything. The flame stands in its glass beside his ear and throws his shadow long across the gravel behind him.

"If I say ‘Throw’ I want you to throw the lantern at one or more of these demon dogs as hard as you can. - we need that lantern to break and cover the beast in oil and light it a blaze. Then: unload the blaster into the damn thing. Do NOT throw it until I give my mark. There are too many variables for anyone to react without thinking through."

Wick looks at the lantern, then at the blaster in his other hand, then at you.

"On ‘throw’."

You go in.

Not straight. You keep to the right-hand silo's side of the gap, wide of Silo Three's corner, the beam out in front of you, and the shed's white light slides off your back and is gone. Inside the gap it is cold, and the walls on either side go up curved and grey into nothing. Gravel under your boots, then packed earth. The blade's indigo hum comes back off the metal close beside you. Wick is at your left, step for step, the lantern at his shoulder, its yellow ring moving with him over the ruts and the silo wall.

Twenty feet, and the gap turns. You swing out round the bend, wide, and the beam comes round with you onto the back of Silo Three: a packed-earth path running along the foot of the wall, the curve of the silo on one side, long grass on the other, knee-high and more, black at its roots. The path goes on along the wall. The beam goes with it until it thins.

You throw the lamp.

It turns over once in the air, the white beam wheeling across the silo wall and the grass, and lands twenty feet on, at the grassy edge of the path, and rolls onto its side. It stays lit. The beam has gone down into the grass and the dirt, and the lamp lies in a pool of its own light, ten feet round, white and close.

You look at what it shows you. The grass at the path's edge, every blade sharp. The grey curve of Silo Three's wall rising up out of the pool. And the packed path, going on past the light, into the dark, the way the prints went.

Nothing moves in it.

Your left hand is empty now. The blade hums in your right, lighting ten feet of earth round your boots. Wick's lantern is the only other light: yellow, thirty feet round the two of you, the silo wall gold where it touches. Behind you, back down the gap, the shed's light is a pale stripe across the lane, fifty feet away.

Out past every light, no sound at all.

details.text:
"Two of them came through here tonight, Wick. We go careful."

Wick looks past you, down the path, the way the prints went. The lantern stays up at his shoulder.

"Two," he whispers. "Not nine."

You look out into the dark, and you listen.

The blade gives you ten feet of packed earth, indigo at the edges. Wick's lantern gives you thirty, yellow, laid gold across the curve of Silo Three where the wall goes up out of the light and keeps going into nothing. Twenty feet on, your lamp lies in its own small white pool in the grass at the path's edge, every blade around it sharp and still. Past all three lights there is only black: no shapes, no edges, no depth to it at all.

Nothing moves in any light. You hold your breath and listen past the hum of the blade and the small tick of Wick's flame behind its glass. Nothing. Not out on the path, not in the long grass, not back toward the gap.

You stand still and wait.

The cold gets into the backs of your hands. Wick breathes beside you, short and quiet. The seconds stretch.

Then, from far behind you, down the rise, out past the shed and the lane and the whole lit edge of the settlement, the voice comes again. Faint. Clear.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words. The same breath before "honey".

Wick goes still. The lantern dips, the yellow ring sliding down the silo wall to his boots, and then it comes back up to his shoulder. He stays at your left.

Out here, nothing else answers it. Nothing near you moves.

You reach for the lamp.

Not with your hand. It lifts out of the grass twenty feet away, still lit, the white pool tearing loose from the ground and swinging up with it, and it comes back along the path to you at an easy walking pace, its beam turning over the dirt and the silo wall, until the grip settles into your empty left hand. Behind it the path where it lay goes black.

Wick watches it come all the way in. He says nothing.

You lift the lamp and put the beam out ahead, and you go.

You sweep it wide as you walk: across the long grass on the outer side, pale and knee-high and more in the white light, back onto the path, out across the grass again. The blade hums low in your right hand. Wick is at your left, step for step, the lantern at his shoulder, the blaster in his other hand.

Once, out at the far edge of the beam, where the grass meets the dark by the end of the long barn, the grass stirs. A slow lean, all one way, as in wind. Then it stands still again.

There is no wind on your face.

Fifty feet. The path runs up to a wall: the end of the long barn, planks and sheet metal, grey and pitted in the beam. Its outer corner is close on your right, and past it the long grass goes on round the side of the building into the dark. In the end wall beside you, about ten feet in from that corner, a small door hangs on a runner. It is shut.

Behind you the path goes back along Silo Three to the bend, and to the gap, and to the shed's light, a long way back now and out of sight round the curve of the silo. Wick's lantern breathes yellow on the planks. Your beam lies white on the door.

Down the rise, nothing calls. Not yet.

details.text:
The end wall of the long barn stands at your back, planks and pitted sheet metal, grey in the light. The small door sits beside you on its runner, shut. The outer corner is ten feet to your right, and past it the long grass goes on round the side of the building into the dark. Wick is at your left, an arm's length off, the lantern up at his shoulder, your blaster in his other hand.

"Did you see the grass move, out at the end of the beam?"

He doesn't look away from the dark. "Something. By the corner." A beat. "Wind?"

You put the beam out over the grass and sweep it slow. Half a minute. The light lays the long grass pale and flat-looking out to sixty feet on the outer side of the path: stems, seed heads, the black between them. Nothing in it moves. The path back along Silo Three runs empty to the edge of the light. Past that, nothing. You listen. Your own breath. The hiss of the blade. The small tick of Wick's lantern. Out there, nothing you can hear.

You toss the lamp underarm with your left hand, fifteen feet, to where the grass stirred.

It drops into the long grass just past the corner and lands nose-on, the beam running away from you along the barn's long side. From where you stand in front of the end wall you can see the lamp itself, a white spill on the corner planks, and the glow lifting off the grass tops beyond the corner. The building hides the rest. Your left hand is empty now. The blade in your right gives you ten feet of indigo light; Wick's lantern gives the two of you thirty feet of yellow.

You look, and you listen, again.

The lamp lies where it fell, its beam out of your sight round the corner. Nothing moves at the edge of what you can see. Then, from round the corner, out past the lamp's light, something heavy goes through the grass. Fast. Low. The long dry rush of stems pushed aside by a body, going away from the barn, out into the field. It lasts two seconds, maybe three.

Then it stops, and there is nothing.

You saw nothing of it. The glow still lifts off the grass past the corner, steady and white and empty. Wick is at your left, the lantern up. Behind you the path runs back into the black toward the gap, and somewhere far down the rise the voice that knows Wick's name has not called again yet.

details.text:
The lamp lies where you threw it, a white spill on the corner planks, fifteen feet off in the long grass. You reach for it without moving your feet.

It lifts out of the stems, still lit, turns once in the air, and comes back along the wall to your open left hand. The glow that was lifting off the grass round the corner goes with it. That side of the barn is dark again. The beam is yours: sixty feet of white wherever you point it. The blade hums in your right hand, ten feet of indigo on the planks.

"Stay at my left. Keep that lantern high."

"Left. High." Wick lifts it. The yellow light climbs the end wall.

You put your ear to the small door, the blade held well away from the wood. Half a minute. The planks are cold against your skin. Nothing behind them: no step, no breath, no fan, no tick of metal. A faint dry smell of grain dust comes from under the door. No draught.

"I'll keep lookout while you open the door."

Wick looks down at your blaster in his hand. "It sticks at the start," he says, low. He pushes the pistol into the right hip pocket of the coveralls, grip up, and puts his gloved hand on the door's edge. The lantern stays up in his left.

You turn out from the wall. The lamp sits loose in your fingers; the blade comes up to guard. You lay the beam on the path and carry it left to right, slow: the packed earth running back along Silo Three, empty to the end of the light; the long grass on the outer side, pale, every stem still, out to sixty feet; the corner. Nothing moves. You hear the blade. The small tick of the lantern. Wick's glove shifting on wood.

Behind you the door gives. A low iron rumble, rollers on a runner, three feet of it, and it stands open. Cold dry air and the smell of grain come out of the dark inside.

You step to the doorway.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Far down the rise behind you, out past the shed and the lane. The same words.

Wick goes still. The lantern dips; the light slides down the wall. Then it comes back up. He stays with you.

You go in. Wick comes in at your left.

The beam goes down a long boarded room as wide as the barn, thirty feet, and does not find the end of it. A board walkway runs down the middle between rows of low slatted beds, grain spread in them like raked sand. Roof posts stand along the walkway. On the end wall beside the door, rakes and wide wooden shovels hang on pegs. Along the right-hand wall a fan housing and sheet-metal ducts sit silent. Glowpanel strips run under the roof beam, dark. There is a switch box on the frame just inside the door, and a hook-and-eye latch on the frame, hanging open. No window at this end.

Nothing moves in the light.

Twenty feet in, a rake lies across the walkway. The bed beside it is raked level on one half and not on the other. A hooded lantern stands on the boards next to it, out.

Wick's light reaches it. He looks at the rake and the dark lantern, and he does not look away. He says nothing.

You put your left forearm to the door's edge, the lamp still in that hand, and push. It rumbles back along its runner and meets the frame. Shut. The hook hangs where it was.

The night is on the other side of the planks now. In here: your blade, your beam, Wick's lantern, the smell of grain, and sixty feet of floor before the dark starts again.

details.text:
You turn the lamp in your hand and push it down into the pocket of your robes, lens first, into the cloth. The beam goes out of the room. What is left of it is a dull white glow through the weave at your hip that lights nothing. The floor shrinks to what the blade and the lantern can hold: ten feet of indigo around you, thirty of yellow, then black.

Your left hand is free. The hook hangs on the frame beside your shoulder. You lift it and drop it into its eye. A small iron click. The door is latched.

You put your ear to the planks again, the blade held off from the wood, and listen out this time. Half a minute. The wood is cold. Your own pulse in your ear.

Then, out in front of the door, low, not far: a breath. Long and slow, let out by something big, lying still. Then nothing.

Farther off, back toward the path, a dry tick of grass. Once. Then again, a little to the side of the first. Then nothing.

You see none of it. There is an inch of planking and a hook between you and the night.

Behind you Wick shifts his weight; the lantern creaks on its bail. He has not heard it. His face is turned down the floor.

"Is there another way in or out of this floor?"

"Cart doors, halfway down on the left." His voice is flat and quiet. "And the hatch at the far end, where the chute comes in."

You look down the floor. Half a minute, the blade low, Wick's lantern up beside you. The walkway runs away from you between the beds, the posts standing along it, grain spread in the slats like sand. Twenty feet in: the rake across the boards, the half-raked bed, the dark lantern standing beside it.

And grain on the walkway. It has spilled off the half-raked bed across the boards in a pale fan. Pressed into the dust of it, one line of boot prints. One person, walking. The prints go on down the walkway, past the rake, out of the lantern's yellow and into the dark.

You listen. Nothing down the floor. No fan, no breath, no step. The long room is silent past the edge of the light.

Your left hand finds the switch box on the frame. You throw the switch.

A click. A buzz under the roof beam. details.text:
The hook sits in its eye beside your shoulder. Behind an inch of planking, the night is quiet again.

"Something's lying outside that door. We stay in here, away from it."

Wick's head comes round to the door. His right hand drops to the hip pocket of the coveralls and closes on the grip of your blaster. It stays there. He does not draw.

"How close?" Barely a breath.

The lantern in his left hand does not dip. The light holds steady on the end wall, on the rakes and shovels hanging on their pegs.

"When did she last work this floor? Would she leave her lantern like that?"

He looks down the walkway at it. "Every day. Before the dogs went wrong." A pause. His jaw works. "No. Not on the boards. Not out here by the grain."

You go down the walkway. The boards are dry and hollow underfoot; the glowpanel strips buzz overhead, a hard flat white that leaves no shadows worth the name. The blade hums low at your right side. Wick comes with you at your left, an arm's length off, the lantern up, his other hand still in his pocket on the grip.

Twenty feet. The rake lies across the boards where it fell or was put down. The bed beside it is raked smooth on one half, ridged and lumpy on the other, the work stopped in the middle of a stroke. The hooded lantern stands on the boards beside it, cold, blue tape wound round its handle.

Wick stops beside it and looks down. He does not touch it.

You crouch at the edge of the spill. Grain lies fanned across the walkway, pale, fine as flour where it has broken, and the prints are pressed into it. Half a minute, the blade held out to the side, away from the dust.

One line. One person. Walking: the steps even, the same length each time, heel and toe both set down, unhurried. Nothing dragged beside them. Every print points the same way, down the floor, away from the door behind you. None come back. And they begin here, at the half-raked bed, beside the rake. Nothing comes in from the door end. Past the last of the light, forty feet on, they go into the dark.

The lamp stays lit in your pocket, a dull glow through the cloth. The Force will lift a thing that lies still; it will not catch or slow one in the air, so there is no softening a throw. Nothing is thrown.

You look at the prints again. The same prints, the same white light, the same line going away from you into the black. Nothing new in them.

The barn is silent. The strips buzz. Somewhere behind you, past the door, the night keeps still.

details.text:
The strips buzz overhead. The rake lies across the boards at your feet; her lantern stands beside it, cold, the blue tape gone grey under the white light.

"Close enough. It's lying still, and the door's latched. Breathe."

"Breathe," Wick says, under his breath, and does: in through his nose, out slow. His right hand stays where it is, closed on the grip of your blaster in the hip pocket of the coveralls. His eyes go back down to his mother's lantern.

You look down the floor.

Half a minute. The blade hums at your right side, held out away from the grain. The walkway runs on ahead of you between the low slatted beds, the roof posts marching down it in a line, everything flat and colourless under the strips for another forty feet. Twenty feet on, in the left wall, the wide double cart door stands shut, its heavy bar leaning on end beside it. Past the last lit strip the floor simply stops being there. Black.

Nothing moves in the light. Nothing moves at the edge of it. You listen and there is nothing to hear: no step, no scrape, no breath, the fans dead in their housing and the ducts silent along the right-hand wall. Only the strips, and the blade, and Wick breathing beside you.

The prints run straight on. Down the middle of the walkway, one after another, past the cart door without turning toward it, past the posts, to the end of the light and on into the black. The air coming up the floor out of the dark is still and cold on your face. No draught.

"The hatch at the far end. Where does it come out? Can it be opened from outside?"

Wick looks down the walkway at the dark. "Out the back, under the chute." He swallows. "There's a bolt, I think. I don't know about from outside."

Then the voice.

It comes from far off, far down the rise, thin through the plank walls, and it is the same. The same words, the same breath in the same places.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Wick's head turns toward the door end. He does not move his feet. "Same words," he says, very low. He stays at your left.

You put your free hand into your robes and draw the lamp out of the pocket, still lit, and lift it. The beam jumps out of the cloth and down the floor, white and narrow, past the end of the strips and into the dark half.

You walk. Forty feet down the boards beside the prints, the lamp up and its beam out ahead, the blade low in your right hand. Wick comes with you at your left, an arm's length off, his lantern up, his hand still in his pocket. The cart door goes by on your left and falls behind. The boards are hollow underfoot. You stop where the last strip ends, at the edge of the dark half; behind you the latched door is sixty feet back, her lantern forty.

The beam goes on without you. It runs down the walkway between the beds, past the posts, under a line of dead strips hanging dark from the roof beam, and finds the far wall, sixty feet on. High up, the mouth of the grain chute comes in through the boards. Below it, low down in the wall, a square hatch. Shut.

Nothing living in the beam. Nothing moves.

The prints go on ahead of you into the light, one by one, for twenty feet or so. Past that, at this distance, the dust lies too faint to make them out. The line is just gone into the pale of the boards.

Silence down the floor. Behind you, sixty feet back, the strips buzz over the rake and the cold lantern. Ahead, the hatch, and the dark on either side of the beam.

details.text:
The last strip buzzes over your head. Past it the floor is the lamp's: one white lane of light down the walkway to the far wall, the hatch at the bottom of it, shut.

"We follow the prints, not the voice. The voice is outside."

"The prints," Wick says, low. He tips his lantern down so its yellow light falls across them, the line of them pressed into the grain dust at your feet, then brings it back up. He stays at your left.

You walk.

Sixty feet down the boards beside the line, the lamp up and the beam out ahead, the blade low in your right hand and held out from the grain. Wick keeps pace at your left, an arm's length off, his lantern throwing its yellow ring around the two of you, his right hand still closed in the hip pocket of the coveralls. The dead strips go by overhead, hanging dark from the roof beam. The boards are hollow underfoot. The light you came out of falls behind you, then away.

The prints do not fade. Walking beside them, you can see every one: down the middle of the walkway, one after another, all the way.

They stop at the hatch.

You stand over it. Behind you now, a hundred and twenty feet back up the floor, the latched door; the rake and her lantern a hundred feet; the cart door eighty, back in the left wall. Here there is only the far wall, the chute's mouth high up in it, and the hatch under it, low and square and planked, about three feet across.

You look at it for a full minute, the beam on it, touching nothing. Your hands are full.

It is shut flush. On this side the bolt runs across its lower edge into a keeper in the wall, and the bolt is drawn back, its shaft clear of the keeper. Nothing else holds it. It hangs from hinges along its top edge; it would swing out, and up, away from you. There is no handle on this side but the knob of the bolt. The shaft of the bolt is worn bright where it slides.

On the sill, and on the boards just inside it, the grain dust is swept bare in a shallow arc, the shape a lower edge makes swinging through it.

You read the prints.

One line. One person. Going one way, down the whole length of the floor, an even walking stride, no hurry in it, no faltering, to the sill. There they stop. Nothing comes back. A small work boot, a woman's size, the ridged sole of a farm work boot, pressed clean into the dust a hundred times over between here and the rake.

You look down the dark half, and listen.

Half a minute. The beam and Wick's lantern between them show it all: the walkway, the slatted beds either side with their grain spread level, the posts, the dead strips hanging whole in their brackets, only unlit. Under the chute's mouth, beside the hatch, a small spill of grain on the boards. Nothing moves. The ducts are silent along the wall. Nothing in the beds has been touched. The only marks in this half of the floor are that one line, and yours, and Wick's.

"Who bolts that hatch at night? Would anyone be out back by the chute now?"

"Mum, mostly." Wick's voice is flat. "She does the beds last." He looks at the prints, at the sill. Then, low: "Nobody should be out there now."

You bend your head to the hatch and listen, your ear close to the planks.

Half a minute. Nothing. No step outside, no breath, no tick of grass. Only the cold along the hatch's edge, and the blade humming at your side, and Wick breathing beside you.

"The cart door's bar is down off its brackets. Who'd have opened that?"

"It's barred every night." He turns his head and looks back up the floor toward it, eighty feet off in the dark of the left wall, where his lantern does not reach. "Always."

Silence. Far back up the floor the strips buzz over the rake and her cold lantern. Here, the hatch, unbolted, and the line of prints stopping at its sill.

details.text:
"She does the beds last. Would she go out this way, to the carts?"

Wick doesn't look at you. He looks at the hatch. "That's how she goes to the carts." Low. "Always that way."

You crouch. The boards creak under your knee. You lay the lamp on its side on the walkway, five feet back from the hatch, the lens turned to it, and let go. The beam runs low across the sill and lands square on the planks: every knot in them, every seam, the bright-worn shaft of the bolt drawn back from its keeper. Your left hand is empty now. The blade hums in your right, held out and away from the grain.

Up the floor behind you the dark comes in closer. Wick's lantern holds a yellow ring around the two of you, thirty feet across, and past that the walkway runs black to where the white strips begin.

"Wick, what was your mother's name?"

"Daria."

He stops. The lantern doesn't move.

"Is," he says. "It's Daria."

You bend to the hatch and put your ear close to the planks.

Cold comes through the seam along its lower edge, a thin line of it against your cheek. The blade's hum. Wick breathing at your left, quick and shallow through his nose. Under all of it, nothing; and you stay, and keep listening.

Then, through the wood. Out behind the barn, on the other side of the hatch, about thirty feet off: a breath. Long. Slow. Let out all the way by something big, lying still.

Nothing follows it. No step. No tick of grass. Only the cold through the seam, and the next breath, if it comes, not yet.

Wick has not moved. His lantern is still up. He is looking at the hatch, at the beam on it, at the swept arc of dust on its sill, and his face doesn't change. He heard nothing.

The hatch is shut. Nothing holds it shut. You have not opened it.

details.text:
"Daria. Good. We'll find her, Wick. Not through that hatch, not yet."

The lamp lies on the boards five feet behind you, its beam flat across the sill. The hatch fills it: knots, seams, the bolt drawn back bright from its keeper. Wick is at your left, an arm's length off, his lantern up.

"Daria Hallan. I'll remember it."

"Daria Hallan," he says back. Low. Like setting something down where he can find it again.

"When she goes out to the carts, does she shut the hatch behind her?"

"It shuts itself." His eyes go to the drawn bolt and stay there. "She always comes back in and bolts it. Always."

The bolt stays where it is. Drawn.

Then the voice. Far down the rise, thin through the plank walls, the same words in the same breaths: "Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Wick goes still. The lantern dips a hand's width and comes back up.

Half a minute. The barn creaks once in the cold. And from behind you, from the other end of the floor, a hundred and twenty feet back through the dark and the white light and the latched door, faint through the planks, comes your own voice:

"That lantern on the boards. Do you know whose it is?"

Your words. Your pitch. The little catch of breath before "whose." Once. Then nothing, and the dark up the floor stays empty.

You crouch at the hatch. The blade hums in your right hand, held out and away from the grain. You set your left palm flat on the planks and push.

It is heavier than it looks. It swings out and up on its top hinge, wood scraping wood, and you hold it there at arm's length, your arm straight, the weight of it pressing back down into your hand. Cold pours in over the sill: wet grass, earth, night. The lamp's beam runs out through the square opening and lays itself flat across the ground behind the barn, sixty feet of it: packed earth worn bare, two deep ruts where the carts turn, and twenty feet out, the long grass starting, pale at the tips where the light catches it and black underneath.

Nothing in the beam. Nothing moving in it. The grass stands still.

Somewhere out there, about thirty feet off, is where you heard something big breathe.

You call into the dark, a loud whisper, the sound going out low over the ruts. "Daria! Daria!"

Wick drops into a crouch at your left. The lantern swings low by the opening, its yellow light spilling over the sill and dying on the earth. "Mum?" Barely more than a breath, out through the hatch.

The grass doesn't move. The beam lies on empty ground.

Wick's voice. His exact voice: the rasp in it, the way it drops at the end.

"Daria."

Once.

Beside you Wick has stopped breathing. You can hear that he has stopped. His lantern hangs perfectly still a foot above the sill.

Nothing comes into the light. Nothing else answers. The hatch is a dead weight in your left hand, the cold running in under it over your knuckles, and the dark past the beam is exactly as quiet as it was before.

details.text:
"That wasn't you. Stay down. Not a sound."

You say it low, at the hatch, your left arm still straight under the weight of it. Wick is crouched at your left, an arm's length off, the lantern a foot above the sill. He nods once. He doesn't speak. The lantern doesn't move.

The beam still lies out over the cart turn: packed earth, the two ruts, the grass beginning twenty feet out, pale at the tips. Nothing in it.

You take your hand away.

The hatch drops. It swings down on its top hinge and hits the frame with a hard flat knock of wood on wood that goes through the boards under your knees. Shut. The cold stops coming in. The lamp's beam, five feet behind you, lands on the planks again: the knots, the seams, the bright shaft of the bolt drawn back from its keeper.

Then, through the planks, muffled, from out behind the barn:

"Mum?"

Wick's voice. His. The same breath under it.

Once. Nothing after.

Beside you Wick is very still.

You look at the bolt and reach for it without a hand. It slides along its staples on its own, steady, and seats in the keeper with a small clean click. Bolted.

"Wick. Breathe. It only says what it's heard. That's your voice, not her."

He lets a breath out. Slow. All the way. He nods.

You stand. The blade hums up with you, a short reach of indigo light around your right side. With your left hand you sign to him: with me. He comes up at your left with the lantern, and the two of you go back up the walkway, boards knocking hollow underfoot, the yellow ring of his light moving with you over the drying beds and the undisturbed grain.

Behind you the lamp lifts off the boards. It turns its beam forward as it rises and comes up the dark after you and into your open left hand. The beam goes out ahead of you now, over the prints in the grain dust, her one line of them going the other way.

Eighty feet. The far end falls back into black behind you. The white of the lit strips starts twenty feet ahead.

The cart door is on your left: two wide plank leaves, shut, the iron brackets either side of them empty, and the bar standing on end against the wall beside them. A squared timber beam, long enough to cross both leaves. Heavy.

You open your left hand. The lamp falls.

It hits the boards with a knock and a sharp tick of glass. It rolls once onto its side and lies still at the foot of the door, still lit, its beam running along the boards across the doorway to the right-hand leaf. A crack runs across the lens. A thin dark line runs through the light where it falls.

And from the other side of the door, close, clear through the planks:

"We follow the prints, not the voice. The voice is outside."

Your voice. Your words, from earlier, where the light ends, twenty feet from this door. The same pace. The same breath before "outside."

Once.

Then, under the hum of the blade and Wick breathing at your left, you hear it. Through the planks, low down, out in the grass about fifteen feet past the door: breathing. Slow. Deep. Two of them, apart from each other, lying still.

Wick's lantern is up. His right hand is on the grip in his pocket. He hasn't moved from your left.

The bar leans against the wall at your elbow. Lifting it level into both brackets will take two hands. The blade is lit in your right.

details.text:
You lift one finger to your lips and look at Wick.

He sees it. He doesn't make a sound.

You go down into a crouch at the foot of the door, the blade held out low at your right side, its hum the loudest thing on the floor. The lamp lies on the boards beside your knee, its cracked beam running across the doorway. Past the planks, about fifteen feet out, the slow breathing goes on.

With your free hand you point him to the far end of the bar, then to the bar itself, then up: the brackets.

Wick nods once. He crosses behind you, low, and sets his lantern down on the boards against the wall under the far bracket. The flame leans and steadies. He takes his right hand off the grip in his pocket. He looks at the bar, then at you, and takes hold of the far end with both hands.

You take your end in your left hand. The blade stays out to your right, clear of the wood and of him.

You tip the beam down off the wall toward him. It comes over slow and heavy and he catches it, and for a moment the whole length of it hangs level between you at the height of your knees, rough grain biting your palm, the weight of it already pulling at the tendons of your wrist.

One finger. You mouth it. One.

Two fingers. Two.

Wick's knuckles are white on the wood.

Three.

You lift.

His end comes up. Yours comes up with it, a foot, more, your left arm shaking along its whole length, and then the beam twists in your one hand and the squared edge rolls out of your fingers.

It drops.

Your end hits the boards with a crash that goes through the whole floor, wood on wood, flat and enormous in the quiet. The planks of the door buzz with it. Wick lets his end down after it, fast, before it can drag him, and it lands with a second, smaller knock.

The bar lies on its side on the boards in front of the door, a foot back from the lamp. The brackets above it are empty. The door is not barred.

Nobody is hurt. Your palm stings where the grain went out of it.

Then, out past the planks, a sound you have not heard yet tonight: something getting up out of the grass. A few soft, quick steps, heavy for how soft they are, going away from the door along the wall to your right, toward the far end of the barn. Then nothing. It has gone down flat again.

You haven't seen anything.

Wick stoops for his lantern. He brings it back up in his left hand, and his right goes back to the grip in his pocket, and he comes back to your left, an arm's length off.

You put your ear to the planks.

The wood is cold against your cheek. It smells of dust and old grain. Through it, under the blade's hum and the small sounds of Wick's lantern, you find them one at a time.

The first is close to the line of the door, a little to your left, about fifteen feet out, low in the grass. Slow, deep breaths. It has not moved.

The second is off to your right now, about fifteen feet out and ten or fifteen feet along the wall toward the far end, where the steps went. It breathes the same way. Slow. In no hurry.

Both of them lying still.

You reach out past the wood with the Force, toward the two of them.

There is the barn. There is the cold. There is Wick, close at your left, wound tight. Out past the planks, nothing comes back to you that you can place.

The far-end hatch is bolted, eighty feet down the dark half. The small door is latched, forty feet back up the floor. Somewhere far down the rise, the voice has not called again yet.

The bar lies at your knees. The door in front of you is shut, and held by nothing.

details.text:
You keep your voice down to almost nothing. Wick leans in to hear it.

"That's on me, not you," you whisper. "You held your end. Again. Both hands this time. On my nod."

He nods. He doesn't say a word.

Your thumb finds the activator. The blade goes out with a short dying hiss and the hum that has filled the floor all this time is simply gone. The quiet that comes in behind it is enormous. The strips still burn white overhead, the lamp still lies lit on the boards at the foot of the door, Wick's flame still leans in its glass. Nothing out past the planks changes. The two of them go on breathing.

You lay the hilt down on the boards at your right knee, slow, metal touching wood without a sound. Close enough to have back in a heartbeat.

Both your hands are empty.

Wick crosses behind you, low, and sets his lantern down against the wall under the far bracket again. He takes his hand off the grip in his pocket and takes the far end of the bar in both hands. His eyes are on you.

You get both hands under your end. The wood is rough and cold and heavier than it looks.

You nod.

It comes up. Your end and his together, off the boards, past your knees, the weight dragging at your shoulders and the small of your back, both arms shaking and holding. Level. Higher. The iron lip of your bracket goes by under the beam, and you let it down.

It drops home into both brackets with a heavy knock of wood on iron that runs through the whole door.

The bar sits across both leaves. The cart door is barred.

Wick lets out a breath. He stoops for his lantern, brings it back up in his left hand, and his right goes back to the grip in his pocket. He comes back to your left, an arm's length off.

You put your ear to the planks.

The wood is cold against your cheek. Through it, without the hum now, the night outside comes in clearer than before: the grass moving a little in the wind, and under it the two of them.

The first is where it was, a little to the left of the door's line, about fifteen feet out, low in the grass. Slow, deep breaths.

The second is where it was too, about fifteen feet out and ten or fifteen feet along the wall to your right, toward the far end. The same slow breathing.

Neither of them moved at the knock. They lie there in the long grass, a door's thickness and fifteen feet from your face, breathing as if they have all night.

You haven't seen anything.

The hilt lies at your knee. The far-end hatch is bolted, eighty feet down the dark half. The small door is latched, forty feet back up the floor. Somewhere far down the rise, the voice has not called again yet.

details.text:
You close your right hand on the hilt where it lies at your knee and bring it up, unlit, cold metal in your palm. Your left hand finds the lamp at the foot of the door. The cracked lens throws its beam ahead of you, a thin dark line running through it.

Wick is at your left, an arm's length off, his lantern up.

You turn your face to the planks and raise your voice, loud, mocking, sing-song:

"I'm a stupid, mutated dog and I couldn't possibly figure out a way to get inside that barn because I'm STUPID."

It booms off the boards and the roof and comes back down the floor at you. Then nothing.

Wick doesn't say a word. His eyes go to the cart door and stay there. In his pocket, his hand closes tighter on the grip.

A few seconds. Then, through the planks, low and close: the grass parts. Something gets up out of it, just left of the door, and moves. Not fast. No growl, no bark, only the long hiss of grass on a body and its breath going with it, ten feet or so further along the wall to your left, toward the small door's end. It goes down again. The grass settles. The breathing goes on, slow, exactly as before.

You sweep the lamp's beam down the floor. The near half lies white and empty under the strips: the walkway, the beds of level grain, the rake and the dark lantern twenty feet up, just as they were. Past where the strips end the beam runs on into the black half over boards and slatted beds and the feet of the posts, sixty feet of nothing, and fades short of the far end, where the hatch is only a dim square, shut. Nothing living on the floor. Through the door at your shoulder you can still hear the two of them breathing: one now about ten feet left of the door's line, the other where it lay, ten or fifteen feet to the right.

You draw your left arm back and throw.

The lamp tumbles up the walkway, its beam wheeling across the roof, the beds, the boards, and hits the small door forty feet away with a flat bang that rings off every wall. It drops at the foot of the door and clatters on the boards. It comes to rest on its side, still lit, the cracked lens holding, its light lying along the boards.

The bang fades up into the roof.

You put your ear back to the planks.

To the right, the grass parts again. The one that lay toward the far end is up and going: low, quick, along the wall toward the small door, right across the front of the door you are crouched behind, close enough that you hear its weight pass on the other side of the planks. Twenty feet or so. Then it goes down again, just left of the door's line, a few feet short of the other. Neither of them makes a sound beyond the grass and the breath. Both lie still. Both breathe slow.

Nothing comes against the small door.

From far down the rise, faint through the walls, the voice: "Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

Wick goes still beside you. His lantern dips, and comes back up.

Half a minute later, from the other end of the barn, beyond the bolted hatch, small and faint down the length of the dark floor, in Wick's own voice:

"Mum?"

Outside the cart door: both now lie about 15 ft out, left of the door's line toward the small door's end, a few feet apart. One moved when you shouted; the other came along the wall at the clatter. Neither came against a door. You have seen nothing.
The two outside the cart door heard your shouted line clearly. The voices outside repeat words they have heard, word for word, in the voice that said them: yours, and Wick's.
Something lies about 30 ft out beyond the far-end hatch. Half a minute after the last call it said 'Mum?' in Wick's voice. The hatch is bolted.
Earlier your own voice spoke once from outside the small door, 40 ft up the floor from here. The small door is only latched: a hook in an eye.
Force Connection reads a creature you can see within 30 ft; it does not find or place what you cannot see. Minor Telekinesis reaches 30 ft: your lamp at the small door is 40 ft off.
The voice down the rise calls every few minutes, the same words. It called just now.

Your blaster is in the right hip pocket of the coveralls Wick wears, grip up, his hand on it. He has never fired a blaster; he has fired a rifle, for vermin. He has said 'On throw'. Your holster is empty.
In your robe pockets: the folding knife (folded), the flat cell, three pairs of work gloves. In your backpack: the canteen, the dead datapad, eight rations. The comm at your collar is closed.
It is about three hours since the sun went down. It will not be light for about twelve hours.

The lamp hit the small door with a bang; at the clatter the other one went low along the wall past the door toward that end and lay down just left of the door's line, a few feet from the first.
